title: Rice Flatsedge: How to Spot and Control Payong Payong in Palay
metaTitle: Rice Flatsedge: Identification and Control in Palay
metaDescription: Rice flatsedge can cut rice yield by as much as 40 percent and hosts blast and sheath blight. Learn how to spot it and control it early in your field.
excerpt: Rice flatsedge, or Cyperus iria, is an annual sedge weed of irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. Farmers call it payong payong, siraw siraw or taga taga. It comes up soon after you transplant or seed your palay. This page shows how to spot it early and how to control it before it sets seed.

heroImage.alt: Rice flatsedge (Cyperus iria), a sedge weed of Philippine rice fields
heroImage.credit: MargaretRDonald, CC BY SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
This damo is a sedge from the Cyperaceae family, and its scientific name is Cyperus iria. Filipino farmers know it as payong payong, siraw siraw or taga taga. You will find rice flatsedge in both irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields.

It is an annual, so each plant lives for one season only. It spreads by seed alone, but it makes plenty of them. Its seedlings also come up quickly once the rice goes in. Because it starts so early, it competes with young rice right from the beginning. That is why early weeding matters most with this sedge. Watch your field closely in the first weeks after transplanting or direct seeding, and pull it before it flowers.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about rice flatsedge
rows: Payong payong, siraw siraw, taga taga
Irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields

blocks.text: Like all sedges, it has a solid, triangular stem with no nodes, while rice has a round, hollow stem with joints. The stems feel smooth. Its leaves are long and narrow, tapering to a point. At the top, it carries an umbrella shaped flower head with many erect spikelets that spread outward. The spikelets range from yellow to yellowish brown, which gives the heads a golden look.

items: Smooth, three sided stems with no joints, easy to tell from rice stems.
Long, narrow leaves that taper to a fine point at the tip.
An umbrella shaped flower head with many erect spikelets spreading outward.
Yellow to yellowish brown spikelets that give the head a golden color.
Seedlings appearing between rice hills soon after transplanting or direct seeding.
Smallflower umbrella sedge shares the name payong payong, but its heads form tight, round balls instead.

blocks.text:
Rice flatsedge is a C4 weed that sets up quickly in the field soon after rice goes in, whether transplanted or direct seeded. One plant can produce 3,000 seeds. When nobody controls it, it can reduce rice yield by as much as 40 percent.

This weed also does harm beyond competition. It can act as an alternate host for other rice pests, such as green leafhoppers. It can also host Pyricularia oryzae, Rhizoctonia solani and Sarocladium oryzae. These fungi cause rice blast, sheath blight and sheath rot, in that order. So a weedy field keeps these pests and diseases close to your palay.

items: Start weeding early, in the first weeks after transplanting or direct seeding, because this sedge establishes soon after the rice goes in.
Pull plants before the yellow spikelets ripen, since it spreads only by seed and one plant can produce 3,000 seeds.
Keep bunds and canals free of it, because it can host green leafhoppers and the fungi behind blast, sheath blight and sheath rot.
Level the field and keep water evenly over the soil, so seedlings have fewer bare, dry spots to come up in.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Sedges

If water and weeding cannot hold rice flatsedge down, choose an active ingredient that works on sedges at the age of your rice. The table follows the PhilRice eDamuhan recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Rice Flatsedge Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before their flower clusters turn brown, since one clump drops a great deal of tiny seed.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [sedge weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.
Not Sure It Is Rice Flatsedge?

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Rice Flatsedge

items.q: What do farmers call rice flatsedge in Tagalog?
items.a: Farmers call it payong payong, siraw siraw or taga taga. Its scientific name is Cyperus iria. Take care, because smallflower umbrella sedge also goes by payong payong and siraw siraw. To tell them apart, look at the flower heads. This weed has spreading, yellowish spikelets, while the other forms tight, round balls.

items.q: How do I control it in my rice field?
items.a: Prepare a well leveled field and keep the water even, then weed early, since it comes up soon after the rice goes in. Pull plants by hand before they flower. Keep the bunds clean as well. If you need a herbicide, choose one for sedges that fits the age of your rice. Always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Can this weed spread rice diseases?
items.a: Yes, it can. It acts as an alternate host for green leafhoppers. It also hosts the fungi that cause rice blast, sheath blight and sheath rot. So weeding it out does two jobs. It removes a competitor, and it takes away a place where pests and diseases can stay near your palay.
